author: blu
body: This chapter used to emit stored blocks only. That was correct RFC 1951 and it was not compression: a stored block is the input verbatim behind a five-byte header, so deflate-compress returned MORE bytes than it was given, and every caller reaching for Gzip -- the de facto name for "make this smaller" -- got a valid gzip stream 23 bytes larger than its input. Nothing caught it for the same reason nothing ever catches a pass-through: the tests asserted a round-trip, and a pipe round-trips perfectly. A ROUND-TRIP TEST CANNOT TELL A COMPRESSOR FROM A PIPE. The tests here now assert the output is SMALLER, which is the one assertion a stored-block implementation cannot pass.

author: blu
body: The matcher is Lz77's, and it now reaches exactly as far as RFC 1951 allows: a 32768-byte window and matches up to 258. It used to stop at 255 and 255, which was never a format limit but the limit of a brute-force scan; Lz77 indexes positions by a hash chain now, so the window costs nothing to widen. Borrowing a matcher we already have and already test beats writing a second one.

author: blu
body: BTYPE=02 (dynamic Huffman, where the code table is built from the data and shipped with the block) closes most of the remaining ratio gap against zlib on skewed data. It is deflate-compress-dynamic, below.

author: blu
body: It chooses per BLOCK, not once per stream. A stream is a sequence of blocks and each carries its own BTYPE, so an input that changes character part-way through -- text then noise, prose then compressed data -- does not have to pay one compromise across both halves. The whole-stream candidates are still built and still compete, so the per-block stream can win but never lose.

author: blu
body: Choosing a block type means measuring three encodings of the same tokens, and the measurement is the encoding: bw-pos counts the bits a writer holds, so a candidate costs exactly what it writes and no separate size model can drift away from the emitter.

author: blu
body: The join is exact because the candidate began in the same phase: its first completed byte IS the byte the real writer was part-way through, so appending its bytes and taking its phase reproduces the stream bit for bit.

author: blu
body: A fixed-Huffman block has no length cap -- only a stored block does -- so a whole input fits in one, and deflate-compress emits exactly that.

author: blu
body: The block itself is written by dfl-fixed-block, which takes a writer and a BFINAL flag and gives a writer back rather than finishing a stream. All three encoders are shaped that way, because per-block type selection needs to put blocks of different types into ONE bit stream: a fixed or dynamic block does not end on a byte boundary, so a chooser cannot concatenate three finished streams, it has to keep writing into the same one.

author: blu
body: It emits from TOKENS rather than driving the matcher itself. The token sequence is what dh-tokenize already produces for the dynamic path, so tokenizing once and encoding it three ways replaces three separate matcher runs over the same input.

author: blu
body: The matcher keeps a hash chain now, so tokenizing carries the two tables. They are built here rather than by the caller because they must not outlive one tokenization -- they are mutated in place, and a pair shared between two calls would offer positions from the wrong input. Callers see the same four arguments they always did.

author: blu
body: Tokenizing a slice of a longer input, with the bytes BEFORE it available to match against. Deflate never needs this -- it tokenizes a whole input at once -- but Brotli cuts its input into meta-blocks and a copy distance there reaches back through everything already emitted, not just through the current meta-block. A matcher started fresh at each cut cannot see any of it, so the window is the meta-block whatever the header declares.

author: blu
body: Seeding walks the history inserting positions without emitting tokens, so the chains point at real earlier positions and the match search is unchanged. The seed is bounded by the matcher's own window, since a candidate further back than that is rejected anyway.

author: blu
body: The same block written into a stream rather than onto a byte array. It aligns after the header, then puts LEN, NLEN and the bytes through the writer, so a stored block can sit between two compressed ones. The padding is charged to the candidate, which is right: mid-stream a stored block costs up to seven bits more than it does at the start, and the chooser should see that.

author: blu
body: Each of the three encoders emits a complete, self-describing stream with BFINAL set, so deflate-decompress reads whichever one it is handed, and picking the shortest of the three is already never longer than the stored block. What that whole-stream pick cannot do is change its mind part-way through an input. One BTYPE has to cover everything, so a file that is half text and half compressed data or noise pays one compromise across both halves: choose dynamic and the noisy half inflates, choose stored and the text half is not compressed at all.

author: blu
body: That is what dfl-chunked does. It cuts the token stream into regions, and for each region writes all three block types into forked writers, keeps whichever came out shortest in BITS, and joins it. Because the candidates all start from the same bit phase the comparison is exact, and because the winner is a writer already holding the encoded block there is nothing to encode twice.

author: blu
body: One tokenization feeds all four candidates. The matcher used to run three times over the same input; now it runs once and the token sequence is encoded four ways, which is the cheaper half of this change.

author: blu
body: Both block types, dispatched on BTYPE. A stored block realigns to the byte boundary and copies verbatim; a fixed block reads symbols until end-of-block.

author: blu
body: A stored block's LEN and NLEN sit on the byte boundary after the header bits.

author: blu
body: The mirror of the dynamic encoder. Read HLIT/HDIST/HCLEN, read the code-length code lengths in their permuted order and build that table, decode the literal and distance code lengths through it (with the 16/17/18 run codes), build those two tables, then decode symbols exactly as the fixed path does but through the data's own codes.
